1) The average composition of organic matter respiration in the NW Ibero-Moroccan upwelling is close to the Redfield ratio, with a slight excess of C over N and P. 2) The composition of the organic matter that mineralizes in the dissolved phase (DOM) and in the particulate phase (POM) is different.

the composition of mineralized dissolved and particulate organic matter in the ocean has a large variability, and the stoichiometry of the decomposition of the different organic matter fractions is not uniform in the NW Ibero-Moroccan upwelling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the composition of the organic matter that is degraded during the first stages of the biological cycle in the NW Ibero-American upwelling, and with the stoichiometry of the mineralization process.
the stoichiometric composition of the products of the early stages of organic matter degradation in the ocean, and with the fate of the biogenic silica produced by the diatoms.
the stoichiometry of the decomposition of the organic and inorganic products of phytoplankton in the NW Ibero-American coastal upwelling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the degradation of dissolved, particulate and hard organic matter is not uniform throughout the upwelling area and is highly influenced by the composition of the phytoplankton assemblage and the physical processes that control particle flux. [2]

in the upwelling system the organic matter is mineralized in three different ways: (1) the organic matter associated with diatoms is degraded in the inner shelf; (2) the organic matter from other phytoplankton groups, including the dissolved fraction, is degraded in the outer shelf; and (3) the organic matter in large particles, which is probably a mixture of diatoms and other organisms, is degraded in deeper waters. [2]

the organic material in the NW IBER upwelling is not a simple mixture of Redfield and non-Redfield material, but rather a mixture of three components: a) the organic material of Redfield ratio, b) a non-Redfield organic component with higher C/N ratio, and c) a non-organic component with a very high C/N ratio.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in coastal systems, the degradation of particulate and dissolved organic matter occurs simultaneously and that the composition of the mineralized material varies according to the nature of the organic matter.
the composition of the mineralized matter is not only a function of the composition of the material, but also of the type of particles involved in the process of remineralization.
the degradation of the dissolved fraction of the organic matter is more intense than expected from a Redfield-like composition.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the composition of the mineralized material is not uniform, and that the composition of organic matter respiration varies with the type of organic matter and the type of particle on which it is found.
the composition of the organic matter that is decomposed in upwelling systems depends on the type of organic matter that is being degraded.

a significant part of the mineralized material is not derived from the dissolved or particulate products of the early degradation of phytoplankton but from large, fast sinking particles that are not sampled by our approach.
